issue: Evidence-label/provenance defect: the sentence states a [1P][FACT] claim (Wan2.2 whole-clip denoising behaviour, and specifically that a later VAE decoder maps the final representation into frames) with no first-party source identified in the sentence — no paper, model card, repository, or datasheet is named. fix_instruction: Name the first-party source explicitly for the Wan2.2 sampling-loop claim (e.g. 'Wan2.2 technical report / model card, HF Wan-AI/... , pinned revision 1ea34ff, retrieved 2026-10-28') or downgrade the label to [1P][DERIVED]/[ILLUSTRATIVE][HYPOTHESIS] with the reasoning made explicit. evidence: Page 32: "The vLLM FP8-KV blog post's often-quoted '54%' — from its Llama-3.1-8B Table 3 (vLLM blog, post dated 2026-04-22 — inside the 2026-08-30 evidence cutoff; retrieved 2026-11-15, an access date only, since access dates are not evidence dates, so no addendum revision applies) [S6] — is, on this book's reading of that table, a decode inter-token-latency (ITL) slope, not a memory ratio or footprint coefficient [1P][HYPOTHESIS]."
issue: Provenance-label mismatch: the sentence labels the interpretation '[1P][HYPOTHESIS]', but [1P] is the Axis-1 provenance value meaning 'first-party: the model vendor's own spec'. The passage itself says the reading 'is the book's own, not a vendor-stated interpretation'. A book-authored reading of a third-party blog table is not a first-party vendor spec; under the book's own axis definitions (Preface: [1P] — first-party: the model vendor's own spec; [2°] — reputable second-hand: textbook, survey, or independent benchmark) the blog is a second-hand source relative to the book, and the book's own interpretation of it is not first-party at all. The same defect recurs in Ch 6 §6.6 (page 154): "the vLLM FP8-KV blog's '54%' [S6] is a decode inter-token-latency (ITL) slope, not a memory ratio or footprint coefficient — on this book's own reading of that post's Table 3, not a vendor-stated interpretation [1P][HYPOTHESIS]". Recurrence sweep: the identical '[1P][HYPOTHESIS]' label is also attached to 'the 8K end is an older-generation and small-tier deployment observation ... this book's reading of the vendor line-ups above, not a vendor statement [1P][HYPOTHESIS]' on page 27 — the same pattern of a book-authored reading being labelled first-party.
fix_instruction: Re-label these three book-authored readings to a provenance value consistent with their source: use [2°][HYPOTHESIS] for the vLLM blog reading (second-hand source) and [canonical scenario][HYPOTHESIS] or [ILLUSTRATIVE][HYPOTHESIS] for the 8K-window reading, which is explicitly 'this book's reading ... not a vendor statement'. Reserve [1P] for the vendor's own stated figures. Sweep Ch 1, Ch 6 and Ch 7 for any other '[1P][HYPOTHESIS]' whose text disclaims vendor statement.

evidence: Page 53: "Decode: required bandwidth, hypothetical single-device aggregate (TPOT ~25 ms) | 5.6 TB/s | 140 GB / 0.025 s — the whole model read once per step on one device (batch-1-equivalent weight-streaming model, before amortization); an aggregate figure, not a per-GPU one [canonical scenario][DERIVED]"
issue: Arithmetic/unit inconsistency across chapters: the 140 GB / 0.025 s figure is quoted with a [canonical scenario][DERIVED] label and with a 25 ms TPOT denominator, but 25 ms is not a canonical-scenario input for this computation — it is the canonical TPOT budget of 25 ms/token, which is [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] (Table 4-2, 'Decode (TPOT) | 25 ms/token | [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION]'), so the derived value inherits an assumed denominator. More materially, the same page states the aggregate figure is 'the whole model read once per step on one device' and then Table 2-2's next row (page 54) computes the 'required bandwidth per GPU (sharded, TP = 8) | 700 GB/s per GPU | 17.5 GB / 0.025 s' — so the chapter carries two different 'required bandwidth' numbers (5.6 TB/s vs 700 GB/s) for the same canonical step, differing by 8×, and the 5.6 TB/s figure is repeatedly quoted in later chapters (Ch 3 mini-case, Ch 6 Table 6-1 '~140 GB weight-read → ~5.6 TB/s rate (batch-1-equivalent)') as if it were the workload's bandwidth demand. The chapter does hedge it, but the labelling and the repeated quotation make the hypothetical single-device number read as a canonical demand. The arithmetic itself (140/0.025 = 5,600 GB/s; 17.5/0.025 = 700 GB/s) is correct; the defect is the label/quotation framing that lets a hypothetical figure carry canonical-scenario authority in three chapters.
fix_instruction: Either relabel the 5.6 TB/s row as [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] (a hypothetical single-device illustration, not the canonical scenario's demand) or add an explicit '[canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] denominator: TPOT 25 ms' note to the row. Where Ch 6 Table 6-1 and the Ch 3 mini-case quote '5.6 TB/s', add the same single-device/hypothetical qualifier at the point of quotation so the number cannot be read as the canonical host's demand.

evidence: Page 95: "the workload's full-utilization (no-headroom) spend is ~$87.6K–$306.6K/mo — ~$146K–$467K/mo on the 70% × 95% + N−1 policy fleet (6 hosts → ⌈6 ÷ 0.665⌉ = 10 provisioned, 9 working; 21 hosts → ⌈21 ÷ 0.665⌉ = 32 provisioned, 31 working; 10 × $14.6K ≈ $146K and 32 × $14.6K ≈ $467K, priced on provisioned hosts because the N−1 spare is paid for)"
issue: Arithmetic defect: ⌈21 ÷ 0.665⌉ = ⌈31.578…⌉ = 32, which is correct as written, but the stated working count (31) then contradicts the same chapter's later canonical statement (page 122, §4.8 mini-case): 'the canonical 40 rps peak (which sizes to ~21 hosts full-util / ~31 working at the 70% × 95% policy (32 with N−1)'. The sidebar's own convention, restated in the same table two rows later, is that 'working = total − 1' for the N−1 spare — so 32 provisioned should imply 31 working. The mini-case's phrasing '~31 working ... (32 with N−1)' is ambiguous but internally consistent only if '32 with N−1' is read as the provisioned total. The real cross-chapter defect is that Ch 4 §4.3 (page 95) states 10 provisioned / 9 working for the 6-host case, while Ch 4's own §4.6 (page 119) says the policy-fleet variant is '10 provisioned hosts at average, 32 at peak' and Ch 16–17's canonical reference (pages 97, 114) prices '~$146K–$467K/mo' — the working-host counts (9 and 31) are never reconciled with the 'ceil the load to whole full-utilization hosts first, then total provisioned = ⌈N ÷ (u × ρ)⌉ and working = total − 1' rule stated on page 122, which yields working = 9 and 31 only if the spare is already inside the 10/32. A reader following the normative rule literally (⌈26 ÷ 0.665⌉ = 40 provisioned, 39 working, as stated on page 122 for the 50 rps variant) cannot reproduce the 10/32 pairing without knowing that the 6 and 21 are already 'full-utilization host counts' including the ceiling — the derivation step is not stated in the table.
fix_instruction: State the two-step derivation inline wherever the 10/32 provisioned figures appear: (1) full-utilization hosts N = ⌈load ÷ 17 slots⌉ → 6 and 21; (2) provisioned total = ⌈N ÷ (u × ρ)⌉ = ⌈N ÷ 0.665⌉ → 10 and 32, working = total − 1 → 9 and 31. Add the same one-line derivation to the sidebar table (page 95) so the numbers are reproducible without jumping to §4.8.

evidence: Page 154: "vLLM KV-offloading (its own 2026-01-08 blog [S7][1P][FACT]) cuts TTFT by 2–22× in a particular warm-cache-hit/reuse benchmark, not a generic cold-cache improvement"
issue: Cross-reference/evidence defect: the [S7] source key is used for a claim attributed to 'its own 2026-01-08 blog', but the Preface states the source keys are 'book-wide, [S1]–[S7]' and Ch 6 §6.3.3 says 'this chapter also uses [S7] (see §6.6), which resolves in the References chapter'. fix_instruction: Name the vLLM blog's first-party URL/revision inline (as Ch 5 and Ch 7 do for pinned sources), and make the label form explicit for blog- and paper-sourced performance claims: e.g. '[S7][1P][FACT] (vLLM blog, 2026-01-08, pinned revision …, retrieved …) — vendor-reported, warm-cache case only'. evidence: Page 100: "Execution occupancy | ~86 / ~344 requests (at Wexec ≈ 8.6 s, where Wexec = 1.08 s prefill + 7.5 s decode = 8.58 s, shown as 8.6 s throughout the book) | [canonical scenario][DERIVED] Little's Law L = λ × Wexec; a separate occupancy from the active-user population"
issue: Internal arithmetic/rounding inconsistency and a downstream contradiction: the ledger says Wexec = 8.58 s but 'shown as 8.6 s throughout the book', and the occupancies are stated as ~86 and ~344 — but λ × Wexec with the rounded 8.6 s gives 10 × 8.6 = 86 and 40 × 8.6 = 344 (matching the printed values), while the unrounded 8.58 s gives 85.8 and 343.2. The chapter's own §4.8 mini-case (page 122) then applies the mixed convention: '50 × 8.6 ≈ 430 requests' — consistent with 8.6 — while Ch 4 §4.3 (page 96) and the canonical-box execution-occupancy row repeatedly present '~344' as the canonical in-flight peak. The rounding is not the material problem; the material problem is that the label [canonical scenario][DERIVED] is attached to a value whose input (Wexec) is itself built on the 1.08 s prefill cap, which Table 4-2 on page 103 labels 'two-term-only upper cap, NOT a feasible deployed prefill target' with 'budget_prefill ≤ 1.08 s − B_other where B_other is positive'. The occupancies (~86 / ~344) therefore inherit an upper-bound status that the [DERIVED] label does not convey, and the ledger row omits it — a defect because these occupancies are the direct inputs to the fleet host counts (⌈344/17⌉ = 21 hosts) quoted throughout Ch 16–17.
fix_instruction: Append the inherited upper-bound qualifier to the Execution occupancy row in Table 4-2 (e.g. 'upper bound: Wexec contains the 1.08 s two-term prefill cap, so B_other is not deducted'), and add the same one-clause qualifier at the first quotation of ~86 / ~344 in §4.3 and at their use in Ch 17's host-count screen.

evidence: Page 130: "Output tokens per dollar (single-stream decode, 50 tok/s) | 9,000 output tokens per dollar | 50 tok/s × 3600 s/hr ÷ $20/hr [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]" and "Total tokens per dollar (serial single-stream floor, no overlap; canonical 25 ms/token basis) | ~199,000 tokens per dollar | 9,500/8.58 ≈ 1,107 tok/s × 3600 ÷ $20; 8.58 s = 1.08 s prefill + 7.5 s decode at the canonical 25 ms/token rate [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]"
issue: Evidence-label/provenance defect and internal inconsistency: the ~199,000 row is built from the canonical 25 ms/token TPOT and the canonical 1.08 s prefill residual, i.e. from two canonical-scenario inputs, yet it carries [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] because the chapter's 'mixed-input convention' lets the non-canonical ~50 tok/s point govern. But the ~199,000 row itself never uses the 50 tok/s point (it uses the canonical 25 ms/token rate), so the mixed-input convention is being applied to a row with no illustrative input at all. Meanwhile the row immediately above it (~242,000) uses the illustrative 20 ms/token rate and correctly carries [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]. The arithmetic itself checks out (9,500/8.58 = 1,107.2 × 3600/20 = 199,300 ≈ 199,000; 9,500/7.08 = 1,342 × 180 = 241,560 ≈ 242,000; 1,583 × 180 = 285,000), so this is a label/provenance mismatch, not a numeric error. Recurrence sweep: the same mixed-input convention is asserted for the whole table on page 131 ('The mixed-input convention therefore governs: the non-canonical input wins, and the rows carry [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] rather than [canonical scenario][DERIVED]') — which mislabels the canonical-input rows.
fix_instruction: Relabel the ~199,000 row [canonical scenario][DERIVED] (its inputs — 9,500 tokens, 8.58 s, 25 ms/token, 1.08 s, $20/hr — are all canonical-scenario values) and restrict the mixed-input convention statement (page 131 note) to the rows that actually consume the ~50 tok/s point (the 9,000 and the ~285,000 rows).

evidence: Page 155: "The resolution is capacity/scheduling — additional hosts, chunked prefill, admission control/backpressure, or P/D disaggregation. The architect re-checks the dashboard an hour later: p95 TTFT is back under 2 s, and the mechanism check confirms the capacity/scheduling change rather than the cache ... Hosts were raised from H = 1 to H = 21."
issue: Cross-chapter consistency / unsupported outcome claim: the mini-case narrates a restored p95 TTFT ('back under 2 s') after raising the host count from 1 to 21, but the chapter's own arithmetic shows that at 21 hosts the peak prefill demand is still oversubscribed — 'the peak prefill oversubscription falls from 18.6× to 51.6 ÷ (21 × 2.77) ≈ 0.9×' — and the page itself concedes 'That p95 restoration is an [ILLUSTRATIVE][HYPOTHESIS] — an expectation from the analytical screens above, pending benchmark confirmation'. A concrete outcome ('back under 2 s') is nonetheless narrated as an observed fact in the mini-case's prose before the caveat, and no measurement is cited, which reads as a measured result inside a chapter whose stated discipline (Ch 6 §6.7, Ch 14) is that goodput/p95 restoration must be measured. The same page also asserts the resolution was 'capacity/scheduling ... rather than the cache' and 'the mechanism check confirms the capacity/scheduling change' — an attribution claim with no instrument named, whereas the chapter's diagnostic method (§6.3.4) is to read counters, not to assert a cause.
fix_instruction: Rewrite the restoration sentence so the status travels with it: e.g. 'the dashboard is expected to return p95 TTFT under 2 s (an [ILLUSTRATIVE][HYPOTHESIS] from the screen, pending the Ch 14 benchmark), since the prefix-cache saving of ≤13% cannot close an ~18.6 host-equivalent gap' — and either name the instrument that would confirm the attribution (prefix-hit ratio, prefill queue depth) or remove the 'mechanism check confirms' clause.
